title: Walmart teams up with popular coffee chain for home delivery
detail:
Walmart teams up with popular coffee chain for home delivery
Aditya Raghunath
Wed, September 9, 2026 at 1:33 PM CDT 4 min read
WMT
Trade Walmart on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Grabbing a morning coffee and a gallon of milk used to mean two separate stops. Walmart just closed that gap.

The retail giant is rolling out a new delivery partnership that puts a familiar coffee and donut brand right inside its shopping app. 

For Walmart (WMT) stock investors, the move signals how far the company's delivery ambitions have grown beyond milk and paper towels.

Here's what shoppers can expect, and why it matters for the company's bottom line.

Walmart partners with Dunkin'

Walmart is expanding its restaurant delivery business through a partnership with Inspire Brands, the parent company of Dunkin'.

The deal lets customers order Dunkin' beverages and food and have them delivered alongside their regular Walmart order.

The rollout starts with about 150 Dunkin' locations that already operate inside Walmart stores. It will soon expand to most of Dunkin's roughly 10,000 locations across the country, including stores unrelated to Walmart.

Walmart is reaching into the broader restaurant world, using its own drivers and app to bring orders to customers' doors.

More Walmart:

BofA points to crucial Walmart numbers most investors ignore

Walmart, Costco, and CVS have a new way to bring you back

Kroger makes a pricing move Costco and Walmart will love

"Our goal is simple: make it even easier for guests to enjoy Dunkin' whenever and wherever they want it," Dunkin' Brand President and Inspire Chief Brand Officer Scott Murphy said. "By bringing Dunkin' into the Walmart shopping experience, we're creating another convenient way for guests to get their favorite beverages and meals at the speed of Dunkin'."

Eligible customers will see Dunkin' appear automatically in the Restaurants tab of the Walmart app, based on their delivery address.

From there, ordering works the same way as any other Walmart purchase, using the checkout process shoppers already know.

Walmart partners with Dunkin'M. Suhail / Getty Images
Walmart takes on DoorDash and Uber Eats

Walmart made its first move into restaurant delivery back in June 2026, when it added Subway meals to Express Delivery in select markets. 

The test proved popular enough that Walmart is now scaling the idea up fast, and Dunkin' is the next big name on the list.

Walmart's pitch is built around a few clear advantages:

A store footprint within 10 miles of about 90% of the U.S. population

An established last-mile delivery network already used for groceries

Millions of shoppers who overlap with Dunkin' and Subway customers

The ability to combine a restaurant order with a regular Walmart cart

A flat delivery fee model instead of the surge pricing common on other apps

title: Deutsche Bank expects European consumer staples to underperform as structural pressures mount

Deutsche Bank expects European consumer staples to underperform as structural pressures mount

Deutsche Bank expects European consumer staples to underperform as structural pressures mount Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

European consumer staples stocks are trading at 18-year lows relative to the broader market, yet Deutsche Bank expects the sector to continue to underperform as consumer spending fails to keep pace with nominal economic growth.

Analyst Tom Sykes said the bank has repeatedly tested the hypothesis that staples would recover but continues to expect consumer wallets to lag nominal GDP, putting pressure on earnings and valuations relative to the broader market.

Consumer staples companies face increased structural pressures and competition, with channel shift emerging as a central issue for household and personal care and food companies as Amazon, Costco and, to a lesser extent, Walmart dominate category growth.

This is putting pressure on the drug channel and increasingly on grocery outside Walmart.

Deutsche Bank said the shift is likely to pressure sell-in rates relative to sell-out in the key US market.

It said it is wary of investment cases based on a US recovery, adding that channel shift is expected to become an increasingly global issue.

The cautious outlook prompted several rating and target price changes. Beiersdorf, the German personal care group, was cut to 'sell' from 'hold' with the target unchanged at €70.

Danone (OTCQX:DANOY)'s target was trimmed to €61 from €63, retaining 'sell'. Haleon PLC (LSE:HLN, NYSE:HLN) target was cut to 320p from 335p, also retaining 'sell'.

Henkel was raised to €81 from €76, keeping a 'buy' rating, while The Magnum Ice Cream Company (EURONEXT:MICC, LSE:MICC, NYSE:MICC) target was lifted to €15.50 from €13.50, retaining 'hold'.

title: The Market Marked AMZN Stock Down. The Numbers Push Back
detail:
The Market Marked AMZN Stock Down. The Numbers Push Back
Trefis Team
Tue, September 8, 2026 at 1:46 PM CDT 4 min read
AMZN
^GSPC
MSFT
META
WMT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by Mohamed_hassan on Pixabay

When a corporate giant appears to trade for less than the average stock after a pullback, investors must look past headline multiples to distinguish a genuine bargain from an optical distortion.

Amazon.com (AMZN), the titan of e-commerce and cloud computing, superficially appears cheap at 20.6 times trailing unadjusted earnings versus the S&P 500 median of 23.2. However, that apparent discount is an accounting artifact: trailing twelve-month net income includes $80.4 billion in non-operating gains—$53.4 billion of which landed in the June quarter alone. Stripping out these one-off windfalls, Amazon trades at roughly 38 times normalized earnings—a notable premium to the broader market, not a bargain multiple.

After a recent 7% pullback from its one-month high and broader underperformance over the past year, the question for investors isn't whether a deep discount is safe to buy, but whether Amazon's underlying operating engine justifies paying a 38x premium amid an aggressive investment cycle.

The Numbers Show Growth, Not Decay.

A quantitative screen for value traps finds no evidence of decay. Amazon's revenue grew 15.8% over the last twelve months, nearly double the S&P 500 median of 8.4%. The company is profitable, and its operating margin is holding steady, not shrinking. Crucially, the earnings are backed by cash, with an operating cash flow margin of 21%. These are not the vital signs of a business in decline. The data points to a healthy, growing enterprise whose stock price has simply disconnected from its operational performance.

The Market Is Focused On A $220 Billion AI Bet.

The market's anxiety is rooted in a single, large figure: the company's plan to spend approximately $220 billion in cash CapEx in 2026. This large investment, raised from a prior estimate of $200 billion due to the rising cost of memory, is dedicated largely to expanding infrastructure across the company to support generative AI and meet surging demand, with the majority directed toward its Amazon Web Services (AWS) division. AWS revenue growth accelerated for the fifth straight quarter to 37%, and it is now a $169 billion annualized revenue run rate business. This spending pressure raises a natural question for investors: Is Amazon Stock's Peak Margin About To Crack?

This is the strongest argument for the value-trap thesis. Rather than a looming risk, cash flow suppression is already here: trailing twelve-month free cash flow has plunged to negative $11.6 billion after two consecutive quarters in the red, as historic capital spending now outstrips even Amazon's 21% operating cash flow margin. With management noting that the "lion's share of capacity in 2027" is largely reserved and demand is locking up capacity into 2028, this massive investment cycle is set to persist—prolonging the cash burn and leaving investors uncertain about when these outlays will translate into sustainable shareholder returns.

title: Walmart Has Gone Practically Nowhere, While Target Is Up 68%. But Only 1 of These Dividend Kings Is a Buy in September.
detail:
Walmart Has Gone Practically Nowhere, While Target Is Up 68%. But Only 1 of These Dividend Kings Is a Buy in September.
Rick Munarriz, The Motley Fool
Tue, September 8, 2026 at 5:37 AM CDT 4 min read
WMT
TGT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

After a few years of watching Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) crush Target (NYSE: TGT), the pauper has become the prince in 2026. Shares of Target are bullseye-red hot, soaring 68% this year. In the other corner, Walmart is a laggard with a 4% year-to-date decline.

The two retail chains have withstood the test of time. They have raised their quarterly dividends for more than five decades. However, which one is the better buy in September? A case can be made for buying both, but the name I'm going with might surprise you.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Right on Target

When you see a stock outperforming against a rival over the past eight months, you might conclude that Target is growing faster than Walmart. You might also assume that it's trading at a higher earnings multiple or packs a lower yield, given the wide performance gap. You would be wrong on all three counts.

Target's trailing revenue has risen a mere 2% over the past 12 months. Walmart's trailing top-line growth at 6.2% is more than three times faster. Target stock is simply bouncing back from a dark space. It will end a run of three consecutive years of declining revenue this fiscal year.

Turning to valuation, Target has a much lower P/E ratio despite the stock's heady ascent. You can buy the "cheap chic" retailer for a reasonable 17 times trailing earnings, less than half of Walmart's multiple of 39.

Both stocks are Dividend Kings, with at least 50 years of annual payout increases. However, Target's current yield of 2.8% is three times Walmart's 0.9%. You're buying into these stocks hoping you're more in capital appreciation than in income, but knowing that there's a good chance the quarterly distributions will keep rising is a plus for both stocks.

Climbing the wall of Walmart

In defense of the country's leading brick-and-mortar retailer, Walmart isn't the laggard if you zoom out a bit more. Walmart's stock has more than doubled over the last five years. Target shares have fallen by a third in that time. Yes, the earnings multiple is higher, and the dividend is lower, but that is because Walmart has historically commanded a healthy premium to the market.

Walmart's all-weather appeal is its perfect cost controls and high-speed inventory turns, which enable it to sell at lower price points than its competitors. Target is coming off three straight fiscal years of slightly declining sales, but Walmart has only had one year of declining sales in the last 47 years.

5 Defensive Stocks to Watch as CPI and the Fed Put the Rally to the Test

Key Points

Interested in McDonald's Corporation? Here are five stocks we like better.

CPI, the Fed's September meeting, and midterm-year seasonality could test a market that remains near record territory.

McDonald's, Johnson & Johnson, and Walmart offer defensive demand profiles that may hold up better if consumers pull back.

Berkshire Hathaway and NextEra Energy add balance-sheet strength, utility income and power-demand exposure to the defensive mix.

The market has enjoyed a strong run this year, despite pockets of volatility and uncertainty. Year-to-date (YTD), the benchmark SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA: SPY) is up about 13%, and heading into the new week, it's only 1.4% shy of its all-time high. But the next couple of weeks bring a cluster of catalysts that could test it. The August inflation report is due this Friday, Sept. 11, and it lands just five days before the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision on Sept. 16.

Either event could move markets sharply, and they arrive back-to-back. On top of that, there is a seasonal wrinkle worth keeping in mind and respecting: 2026 is a midterm election year, and history shows that midterm years have often produced some of the sharpest intra-year declines, frequently in the autumn, before markets recover strongly once the vote passes.

→ 3 Under-the-Radar Defense Stocks With Record Backlogs

None of this is a reason to panic, and it is certainly not a forecast that stocks will fall. It is simply a reminder that preparation is rarely a bad idea in the markets. If the market's response to CPI, the Fed, and the political calendar turns sour, it helps to know which stocks have historically weathered volatility better than most. The five names below are not the sort that double or triple in value during a bull run. Several of them have even lagged the market this year. But they share the defensive qualities, steady demand, low volatility, and, in most cases, dependable dividends that tend to help them hold their ground when the broader market struggles or turns sharply lower.

McDonald's: The Trade-Down Effect

McDonald's (NYSE: MCD) is one of the market's classic defensive holdings, and the reason is counterintuitive. When household budgets tighten, consumers do not stop eating out entirely; they trade down, swapping pricier restaurants for the value and convenience of fast food. That dynamic can actually lift McDonald's traffic during economic soft patches, giving it a rare quality. A business that can hold steady, or even benefit, when discretionary spending elsewhere dries up.
